extracted.intended_audience: students and researchers in pragmatics, cognitive linguistics, and communication studies (also researchers of humor and discourse)
extracted.subtask_description: A scholarly overview of Relevance Theory (Sperber & Wilson) summarizing its core claims, principles, empirical tests, theoretical debates, and applications (including humor, media, literature, translation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle of Relevance (cognitive)
rubrics_metrics.description: Human cognition tends to be geared to the maximisation of relevance: humans are endowed with a biological ability to search for the most relevant information from incoming stimuli.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Relevance is a property of stimuli that results from a positive balance between the interest (positive cognitive effects) provided and the mental effort required to process the stimulus. This evolved mechanism predicts automatic activation of potentially relevant stimuli, memory retrieval of potentially relevant assumptions, and spontaneous inferential processing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Communicative Principle of Relevance (two clauses)
rubrics_metrics.description: Every act of ostensive communication communicates a presumption of its own optimal relevance, operationalized in two clauses: (a) the ostensive stimulus is relevant enough to be worth the addressee's effort to process it; and (b) the ostensive stimulus is the most relevant one compatible with the communicator's abilities and preferences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clause (b) explicitly includes that the stimulus is the most relevant one the communicator is WILLING AND ABLE to produce; communicators cannot be expected to go against their interests or produce stimuli they are unwilling/unable to produce.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of relevance of an input (effect vs effort)
rubrics_metrics.description: Relevance of an input involves: (a) everything else equal, the greater the positive cognitive effects achieved by processing the input, the greater its relevance; and (b) everything else equal, the smaller the processing effort expended to achieve those effects, the greater its relevance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Positive cognitive effects include adding new information, revising assumptions, or deriving new conclusions from combining old and new information (contextual implications). Assessment of relevance is a balancing of effect (benefit) against processing effort (cost).

rubrics_metrics.name: Relevance-guided interpretive procedure (accessibility and stop rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: Hearers consider interpretive hypotheses in order of accessibility (path of least effort) and stop when they arrive at an interpretation which satisfies the expectations of relevance raised by the stimulus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a first interpretation is considered a candidate to match the intended interpretation, the hearer will stop at this point in the absence of contrary evidence. Experimentally, one can manipulate either processing effort or the order of accessibility of competing interpretations to test this.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inferential model over code model
rubrics_metrics.description: Utterances are not simply encoded/decoded; decoding plays a minor role compared to the inferential activity of the interpreter. Utterances are pieces of evidence about the speaker's meaning rather than automatic conveyors of it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comprehension begins with identification of logical form (schematic coded input) which is then enriched inferentially into explicatures and implicatures. This emphasizes the primacy of inference in deriving speaker meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explicit/implicit distinction and mutual parallel adjustment
rubrics_metrics.description: Explicitly communicated information (explicatures) and implicitly communicated information (implicatures) both require contextualization; explicatures may include items Grice counted as implicatures. RT rejects strict dual-stage (literal-then-implicature) processing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicatures and implicatures can have degrees (strong/weak) depending on addressee responsibility and processing required. Some cases (debated) may be termed impliciture by others; RT favors mutual, parallel adjustment of explicit and implicit content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conceptual versus procedural encoding
rubrics_metrics.description: Linguistic forms may encode two types of information: concepts (conceptual representations) and procedures (instructions for manipulating concepts).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedural meaning (e.g., some connectives, discourse markers, intonation) constrains the inferential process by indicating the kind of inferential operations required, thereby reducing overall effort. Recognizing procedural items is a criterion for analyzing discourse flow and reducing inferential cost.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ad hoc concept formation
rubrics_metrics.description: Addressees may construct ad hoc concepts online in response to specific expectations of relevance; these concepts are not lexically given but are created to fit context-specific interpretive needs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ad hoc concepts increase the salience of certain encyclopedic assumptions and differ from lexicalized concepts in being context-sensitive; this mechanism is central in accounts of metaphor and other figurative language within RT.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mutual manifestness (vs mutual knowledge)
rubrics_metrics.description: Replace the notion of mutual knowledge (which generates infinite recursion) with mutual manifestness: what is manifest is what one is capable of inferring or perceiving, even if one hasn't done so yet; communication makes certain assumptions mutually manifest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mutual cognitive environment is the subset of cognitive environments shared as mutually manifest assumptions. Critics argue this may reintroduce mutual knowledge under another name; RT maintains the functional distinction for pragmatic analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Communicated vs non-communicated acts
rubrics_metrics.description: Communicated acts depend on the addressee's perception that a particular speech act has been performed (e.g., admitting, promising); non-communicated acts do not require identification of a particular speech act and rely on recovery of adequate cognitive effects (e.g., predicting, warning).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This distinction has been debated: some argue that acts affecting social environment (e.g., warnings) should be treated as communicated because recovery of social-relational information is essential to comprehension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Irony as echoic attitude
rubrics_metrics.description: An ironic utterance is an interpretation of another thought/utterance/assumption which the speaker attributes to someone (or self at another time) and simultaneously expresses a dissociative attitude toward it; irony is necessarily echoic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Echoicity involves referring to an attributed thought and expressing attitude (dissociation). Some authors contest that irony can be non-echoic; RT authors maintain echoicity is required for ironic interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modularity and the pragmatic module
rubrics_metrics.description: The mind's architecture includes evolved modules; a pragmatic module (a sub-module of theory-of-mind) is specifically activated by ostensive communication and constrained by the Communicative Principle of Relevance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The pragmatic module is biologically endowed, domain-specific, and automatic in its activation by ostensive stimuli. The central processor itself may exhibit modular properties; modularity informs expectations about automaticity and encapsulation in pragmatic processing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relevance-theoretic account of humor (accessibility + invalidation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Humor is characterized by the mental processes of the audience: the humorist predicts and manipulates hearers' selection of an accessible interpretation which is then invalidated by later material, producing a surprising covert interpretation that yields homogeneous interpretation and amusement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many jokes present initial material with multiple graded interpretations leading the hearer to select an overt (relevant) interpretation; a subsequent part forces reevaluation toward a covert interpretation that becomes the correct, humor-generating reading. Producing humor thus involves controlling accessibility, expectations of relevance, and timing of invalidation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical testing criteria for relevance theory
rubrics_metrics.description: The central claims (cognitive and communicative principles) can be tested by manipulating either processing effort or the order of accessibility of competing interpretations, or by changing the effect factor to make specific interpretations more/less likely to satisfy relevance expectations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experimental designs cited include manipulating content/context to vary effort and effect (e.g., selection tasks, rounded time answers) and observing whether subjects follow relevance-guided interpretive procedures; these provide criteria for empirical validation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grammar as constraining interpretive choices
rubrics_metrics.description: Within RT grammatical attributes are not fixed intrinsic properties but constraints on the choice of candidate (intended) interpretations; grammatical organization plays a role in cognitive contextualization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Grammatical aspects (connectives, conditionals, modals, adverbials, tense, article, etc.) should be analyzed in terms of how they constrain inferential options and affect accessibility/effort in deriving explicatures and implicatures.
